name: Renaissance
summary: The Roman orders, the round arch and the dome return, set by number. Brunelleschi, Alberti and Palladio made proportion into a rule: each part is a simple fraction of the whole, and the building is a calm, symmetric order.

philosophy.core_thesis: Beauty is number: a building is right when each part is a simple ratio of the whole, as in the human body and in music.
design_principles: Set every room and opening in a simple ratio: 1:1, 1:2, 2:3, 3:4 or 4:5, and use the same ratio again in the elevation.
Use the classical orders in their order of weight: Tuscan or Doric at the base, Ionic above, Corinthian at the top.
Compose the front on one central axis, with a bilateral balance and a central entrance or pediment.
Use the semicircular arch and the hemispherical dome; the dome diameter equals the height from the floor to the springing.
Make the column diameter the module, and set the bay at 3 to 5 modules; the storey height at 8 to 10 modules.
Rank the floors: a rusticated base, a tall piano nobile with the largest windows, and a shorter attic.
anti_patterns: Asymmetric fronts with no central axis
Curved, broken or twisting classical elements
Dense surface ornament that hides the order
Proportions chosen by eye with no ratio
Steel or glass skins with no orders and no wall

massing.form: A compact cube or a square-plan palace around a courtyard; a central-plan church of a square or circle under a dome.
massing.proportion: A palace front of 2:1 to 3:2 width to height; a villa is a cube, with a central block and a portico.
massing.roof: A low hipped roof behind a cornice, or a hemispherical dome on a drum; a pediment marks the centre.
massing.relation_to_ground: A rusticated base of one storey, 4 to 6m high, a flight of steps to the portico, and an axial approach.

structure.system: Load-bearing masonry in brick and stone, with barrel and groin vaults and domes on pendentives.
structure.span_and_module: The column diameter is the module; bays of 3 to 5 modules, rooms of 1:1 to 3:2 and spans of 5 to 9m.
structure.expression: The orders show the load: pilasters, entablatures and arches state where the wall carries its weight.

materials.finish: Calm and matt: smooth stucco in warm white, with grey or white stone for the orders.

facade.composition: A flat, symmetric front in horizontal tiers, with an order for each tier and one central doorway or portico.
facade.openings: Round-headed or pedimented windows, 1:2 in ratio, in regular rows; the window-to-wall ratio is 15 to 25%.

light_and_space.daylight: Even, soft daylight from regular windows and a central oculus or lantern.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: An axial route from the portico through the hall to a central domed room; each room is a simple solid.
light_and_space.interior_character: Coffered ceilings, frescoed walls, pilasters and a marble floor in a geometric pattern.

ornament.attitude: Ornament is the classical order itself: the column, the entablature and the pediment, used with measure and restraint.

rules.rule: Fix every dimension by simple ratios: 1:1, 1:2, 2:3, 3:4.
Compose the plan and the front about one central axis.
Set the bays at an equal interval, and use the column spacing as the module.
Stack the orders by weight: Tuscan or Doric below, Ionic then Corinthian above.
Derive the openings, the arcades and the rooms from one module.
Fit the height of the room to the human figure and the width of the room.

images.title: Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio, Rome

emotion.target_response: Harmony and calm: the viewer feels a clear human order, measured and in balance.

avoid_when: The brief asks for curves, drama or movement in the facade.
The programme needs a free plan or a glass skin.

modifiers.how: Bend the front into convex and concave curves, break the pediment, double the columns and raise the light contrast.

canonical_works.work: Basilica of San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice

sources.title: Rudolf Wittkower, Architectural Principles in the Age of Humanism (Warburg Institute, 1949)
Andrea Palladio, I quattro libri dell'architettura (1570)
